summary: Describes the standardization collaboration between the Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) and the IETF.

eli5.summary: Two groups that make rules for phones and the Internet agree how to work together so their rules fit.

questions: how do mobile and internet standards coordinate
subtitle: Framework for coordination between mobile standards (OMA) and Internet standards (IETF).

tldr.problem: The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) and the IETF both develop standards that affect modern communications systems, but they operate independently with different rules, approval processes, and intellectual property policies, risking duplication and incompatibility.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC establishes principles and procedures for coordination between the two organizations: document sharing, formal liaison roles, working group participation, and consultation on mutual interests while each organization retains its own governance.
tldr.outcome: OMA and IETF can now collaborate informally through working groups, escalate issues through designated liaisons when needed, and share information to avoid duplicating work while respecting each organization's independence.

today: RFC 3975 is Informational and describes the standardization collaboration framework that has been in effect since 2005. IETF and OMA continue to coordinate on standards affecting mobile Internet systems.

sections.title: Two Standards Bodies, One Goal
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) develops standards for the Internet and is open to anyone. The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) develops standards for mobile systems and is led by member organizations. As mobile devices and the Internet converge, both bodies develop standards that affect the same systems.

For example, both OMA and IETF specify how phones should handle email (SIP, SMTP), web access (HTTP), and other services. Without coordination, the same capability might be standardized twice with incompatible solutions, or one organization might standardize something that breaks the other's work. This RFC creates a framework for the two organizations to work together while maintaining their independence.
sections.eli5: IETF makes rules for the Internet. OMA makes rules for phones. When phones use the Internet, the rules have to work together.

sections.title: Principles of Cooperation
sections.content:
The RFC establishes that OMA will prefer to use IETF standards unchanged when possible, and will communicate directly to IETF working groups if changes or additions are needed. IETF may ask OMA questions about requirements to better understand mobile needs. The goal is to avoid duplication: if IETF already standardizes something, OMA should build on it rather than create an alternative.

Both organizations will operate according to their own rules, including intellectual property policies, approval processes, and procedures. This framework is a guide for collaboration, not a binding agreement that either party must follow in all cases. Either organization can withdraw from the framework if it becomes inapplicable.
sections.eli5: OMA will try to use IETF rules when they work. If not, they'll ask IETF to fix the rule so it works for phones. Each group keeps its own decisions and processes.

sections.title: Sharing Drafts and Tracking Dependencies
sections.content:
All IETF documents are public on the IETF web site, and OMA technical contributions are published on the OMA web site. Both organizations encourage sharing of draft documents of mutual interest to allow early feedback and avoid incompatible solutions.

OMA and IETF will maintain and exchange, on a regular basis, a list of dependencies: which of each organization's specifications require, build on, or could conflict with the other's work. This visibility helps both organizations spot conflicts and coordinate timing.
sections.eli5: Both groups share their drafts so everyone can see what's coming and point out conflicts early.

sections.title: Designated Liaisons and Formal Communication
sections.content:
Each organization appoints one or more liaison individuals to serve as initial contact points for the other organization's administrative and strategic matters. The IETF's liaison (appointed by the Internet Architecture Board) acts as the entry point for OMA communications to IETF and can report OMA activities and liaison statements to appropriate IETF leadership. The OMA liaison similarly serves as the contact point in OMA for IETF matters.

For most technical matters, working group level discussion is preferred. When that is insufficient, formal Liaison Statements can be exchanged. All IETF liaison statements are published as public documents. OMA members may contribute to IETF under IETF's intellectual property policy, and IETF participants who are OMA members may contribute to OMA under OMA membership rules.
sections.eli5: Each group picks someone to be the other group's main contact. For big decisions, they send formal messages and tell everyone what they said.

sections.title: Open Participation and OMA Involvement in IETF
sections.content:
IETF participation is completely open. OMA members and delegates can attend IETF meetings and subscribe to IETF mailing lists to understand IETF work and provide input on OMA needs. This open participation allows OMA to influence IETF direction and receive informal guidance on using IETF standards.

OMA meetings are normally closed to OMA members only, but IETF may send a representative to OMA Technical Plenary and working group meetings by prior written invitation. The RFC recommends that technical discussions happen on open IETF mailing lists where possible, since OMA's own mailing lists are not open to the public.
sections.eli5: OMA people can join any IETF meeting and discussion. IETF can sometimes send someone to OMA meetings if invited.
